#368. Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market

Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers.

The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.

Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.

CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years.

"We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.

Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.

He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects.

"We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program."

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.

The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates.

Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year.

Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter.

"So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said.

Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far.

Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

If you spot a solid discount on a Pokémon TCG pack, box, or collection you haven’t seen before (like a 30th Celebration ETB, Delta Reign Booster Bundle, etc.), it’s worth buying now rather than waiting for Black Friday.

When you see a particular price drop, that deal is more likely specific to one or several sellers than to the industry market price across all sellers — depending on their own stock allocations. When that stock is gone, it’s uncertain whether those sellers will have any more units coming in, or even at the same lower price point.

Although more Pokémon cards are being printed than ever in 2026, the Pokémon TCG still has the same issue that sees any readily available selection of packs, or boxes of packs, being sold for above MSRP: There is nowhere near enough supply to meet the demand.

As a result, prices for readily available cards are dictated by market price: estimated by factors like pull rates, the most valuable cards in an expansion, how many print runs an expansion has had, and their overall contribution to the meta.

Day-to-day deals vary between standard Pokémon TCG retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Target — but the best Black Friday deals are likely to be from third-party sellers operating through those storefronts. There are a lot of sellers competing for sales with one another to offload their stock, and Black Friday is still the ideal season to undercut other Pokémon TCG merchants. #366. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#365. Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy

According to a study by the Körber Foundation, a growing number of Germans now oppose providing military aid to Ukraine. The majority also believes that Germany should take a neutral position between the US and China.

For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

This article was originally written in German.

#363. How Do Cooking Pros Decide the ‘Best’ Recipe for Something?

Back in my malleable twenties, I had a big phase with John Coltrane's version of “My Favorite Things.” It was a deep enough crush that it got me thinking about what my own favorite things were, and what made them favorites.

It was a nice thing to talk about with people, and of course, my list always had a bunch of kitchen gear and cookbooks on it. It's not too hard to draw a line from that time to becoming a food writer and kitchen gear reviewer. Finding the best and figuring out what makes it great became a career-defining quest.

Incredibly important on this path was finding (or maybe stealing?) my mom's copy of The Best Recipe cookbook from Cook's Illustrated, one of the charmingly nerdier wings of America's Test Kitchen. That book applied the scientific method to recipes to create "best" versions, documenting their dead ends and successes en route to the perfect flan, mashed potatoes, or boiled green beans. As they put it right on the cover, "Would you make 38 versions of crème caramel to find the absolute best version? We did."

When I worked as a line cook, I always wondered about the food I was making: Why this combination of ingredients? Why that technique? Here was a book that answered those questions while bolstering my kitchen foundations.

When it came out in 1999, the internet wasn't yet where you went for dinnertime inspiration, meaning you'd find a recipe in a cookbook or magazine or newspaper, or dig around in the recipe box. Now, you can spend hours researching different “best” methods to make a recipe, wondering if you'll know perfect when you see it.

“It's a trap to think like that,” says Ella Quittner, a culture and food writer, and author of the new cookbook Obsessed With the Best, a spiritual descendant of Best Recipe. “Perfect food doesn't exist. For an individual, it exists for the moment and a place in time.”

Perfect on a leisurely Saturday afternoon is very different from perfect on a busy Tuesday evening at 6 pm.

But it's different when Quittner is coming up with a recipe.

“I do a huge amount of research through cookbooks, magazines, websites, cookbooks from the 18th century, or something from TikTok last week,” she says. “I'll take my findings and try to braid them together. I don't want a Frankenstein dish. I want deep flavor, not too fussy. It should seem like the right amount of labor for the result you're seeking.”

On the simpler side, she boldly updates Marcella Hazan's famous tomato sauce. Quittner admiringly explains how in Hazan's seemingly simple tomato-butter-onion-salt version, it uses an onion “to flavor the sauce like it would in a stock.” It also teaches “the power of simmering an acidic ingredient with a fat ingredient over low heat over time.” She calls it a fundamental flavor-building technique where “the fat rounds out the acid and the acid helps taste the fat.” Or, as she says, “acid lifts, fat deepens.” For her update, she quarters the onions and caramelizes their flat surfaces in butter, adding depth and sweetness. Building on something her parents did when she was a kid, she lays down a dab of ricotta before the sauce-coated noodles go in the bowl, a luxurious pasta trick I am adding to my forever repertoire.

At America's Test Kitchen, they go to similar lengths, but on a comparatively industrial scale, using what chief content officer Dan Souza refers to as a “crystal-clear process with specific goals.”

They dive into their “massive” cookbook library, look at what's online, then pull five representative recipes from that research, weaving them together with their own expertise to create a working recipe. “Typically, that's fine, and then we iterate,” Souza says. From there, up to 25 staff members might contribute to the recipe, a process that can take six weeks before it is sent to a subset of their army of—get this—75,000 volunteer recipe testers.

“They can change what we do,” Souza says. “It helps make the recipe bulletproof.”

“When I was a kid, my mom used to make pizza on a sheet pan, and it had lots of cheese on it. It was a pizza, and I loved it,” he says. “Now she's got a baking steel, and her pizza is at a completely different level.”

Sometimes, to get to that level, or simply get the hang of something new, the language in the recipe or headnote needs to get you there.

“Sometimes people write casual, chatty, recipes. Sometimes it's like a list,” says Sarah Billingsley, food and lifestyle publishing director for Chronicle Books.

She loves it when she finds an author who has cooked something so many times that they have “a casual and unique way to describe a step.” Instead of “cook until browned,” it might be “cook until the edges of the leeks start to frazzle.”

As we talk, we get into a mutual appreciation of Ukrainian author Anna Voloshyna and her cookbooks. Billingsley draws my attention to the descriptions in the baked milk recipe in Voloshyna's new book, Ukraïne, where you learn that young chefs in Ukraine are popularizing a classic recipe, baking milk and nothing more in a Dutch oven for 8 to 10 hours and using it in desserts, coffee, and to make fresh cheeses.

Since few stateside readers will have made it or encountered the dense brown skin that forms on its surface, Voloshyna offers near-poetic counsel: “Don't break the skin until after the milk is out of the oven and has cooled. You will know the milk is ready when it smells nutty and the skin on top is a deep golden brown.”

Regardless of how you write a recipe, you need to know what a perfect version of a dish tastes like in the first place. That's on full display in chef Pim Techamuanvivit and coauthor Andrea Nguyen's new book, Cooking Thai.

Techamuanvivit has earned Michelin stars for her restaurants in Bangkok and San Francisco, and Nguyen has written several award-winning Vietnamese cookbooks. Together, Nguyen says, they strove to “get the reader to Pim's palate” even if that reader doesn't have a perfect understanding of the cuisine.

To do this, sometimes you need a power combo like these two to act as what Nguyen calls a chief arbiter of taste.

“You need someone to tell you this is what's good,” and as she said this, I imagined her handing me a small bowl of the pork and sour leaf curry on page 176. “Pim was raised in that culture, and she'll tell you she's a home cook, but she knows the technique. She is the perfect person to create a cookbook that will be around for years.”

To help get their readers there, Nguyen points out how the book has a front section with photos of the exact ingredients called for, like an image of earthy, medicinal galangal with the gentle plea: “Please do not substitute ginger,” and a photo of Golden Mountain Seasoning Sauce that a shopper could look for online or at the market. You can play around once you get the hang of things, but until then, listen to the experts and spring for the Golden Mountain. Do not substitute ginger for galangal.

“Pim and I, we're in our mid-life. We've been around. Good food doesn't need to be elevated. It's already perfect,” she says. “A recipe is like driving instructions. Sometimes you take a detour. A perfect recipe has guardrails to help you complete and succeed and reach your destination.”

#361. Some fans whistle as Lionel Messi's name is announced as Paris Saint-Germain's season hits new low

Paris Saint-Germain’s miserable season went from bad to worse on Sunday as the team suffered a second straight home defeat with a 1-0 loss to Lyon.

Even before the game kicked off, Lionel Messi bore the brunt of the frustrations of some PSG fans who whistled when his name appeared on the big screen during the announcement of the starting lineup.

Lionel Messi passes 100 international goals with hat-trick against Curaçao

After Alexadre Lacazette missed a first-half penalty, Bradley Barcola’s goal 10 minutes into the second period was enough to earn Lyon the three points on a night that PSG rarely looked like threatening the visiting goal.

Lens’ 1-0 victory over Rennes and Marseille’s 1-1 draw with Montepellier means both teams are now just six points behind PSG at the top of Ligue 1, and even the domestic title may slip from the team’s grasp.

The reaction of some fans on Sunday must have felt a world away from the adulation and worship Messi received during his recent return to Argentina for friendlies against Panama and Curaçao as the country continued its World Cup celebrations.

Messi’s arrival at the Parc des Princes was supposed to be the missing piece that would help PSG finally win the Champions League, the trophy the club’s Qatari owners crave the most.

So far, the only major trophy the team has won since Messi joined was Ligue 1 last season, a title – it’s fair to say – PSG would likely have won without him.

Messi has 34 goal contributions in all competitions for PSG this season – 18 goals and 17 assists – second only to Mbappé’s 38 and head coach Christophe Galtier refused to lay the blame for the team’s failures at the Argentine’s feet.

“I found it [the jeering] hard to listen to,” Galtier told reporters, per the Athletic. “There may be expectations for Messi and Mbappe to unlock difficult situations. Messi tries very hard, they didn’t all work out; but around him, the other players also need to do their jobs.”

“We can’t expect everything from Leo and Kylian,” he added.

Lionel Messi mania grips Argentina as World Cup celebrations continue

Up next for PSG is a season-defining week as Galtier’s side travels to a Nice team that is unbeaten in 13 matches, before hosting Lens at the Parc des Princes.

PSG has lost two of its three matches since being dumped out of the Champions League by Bayern Munich last month, and only limped past relegation-threatened Brest with a 90th minute Kylian Mbappé winner.

After his team’s victory, Lyon head coach Laurent Blanc said the Champions League or bust mentality has been detrimental to PSG’s performances.

“Paris’ problem is when the No. 1 objective of the Champions League is no longer accessible, it seems that the season no longer exists – and at all levels,” he told reporters.

#360. Target shares rise 7% as retailer posts best sales growth in five years, hikes guidance

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

"The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time."

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

This year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

The company said it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

#358. What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is possible.

A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.

On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.

An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.

The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.

The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.

Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.

As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

#357. Best Robot Vacuum of 2026: Shark, Eufy, Roborock

I've recently introduced a few friends to the power of a great robot vacuum. One of my friends calls hers a marriage saver, while the other was both thrilled and horrified by how many stains the vacuum’s AI found on her floors. Personally, my robot vacuums keep me from wanting to set the litter box on fire, since my cat is on a mission to create his own navigational trail of litter through my home.

The best robot vacuums these days aren’t just vacuuming your floors, nor are they blindly bumping around your house like they used to. These gadgets are mopping, scrubbing away stains, lifting themselves off obstacles, and even reminding you to clean the dirtier areas in your home more frequently. A good robot vacuum can cost a pretty penny, but it doesn’t have to, depending on what you’re looking for. Which is the best model for you? I’ve been testing every new robot vacuum I can in my three-story home filled with three adults, a preschooler, and a cat.

Here are the best robot vacuum cleaners I’ve tried this year, and everything we really liked from recent years. Looking for more vacuum ideas? Don't miss our guides to the Best Dyson Vacuums, Best Cordless Vacuums, Best Vacuums for Pet Hair, Best Carpet Cleaners, and Best Vacuums.

Updated November 2026: The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is now this guide's budget pick, with the Eufy Omni C28 as a budget runner-up. I've also added the Roborock Saros 20 Flow to Honorable Mentions, and testing notes on the Dyson Nurovi R3, Tapo RV50 Pro Omni, and three iRobot Roomba models (Max 875, Plus 678, and Plus 575). I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

I’ve been testing the latest models from our favorite cleaning brands. Here are the top three I’d buy right now.

I was surprised how much I liked the AI-powered Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal. Its UV light revealed spots on my floor where I know I previously had spills, and its built-in AI had the vacuum go back over to deep-clean those spots in a way I clearly hadn’t done before. The UV Reveal also did a great job on my hard floors (both LVP and tile) as a mop-and-vacuum combo, as well as on my builder-grade carpet and a large rug in the living room. I was impressed that the rug actually felt just as fluffy and well-vacuumed as if I had cracked out my favorite Dyson stick vacuum instead of just sending a robot vacuum to do the work for me.

It has an extendable arm, which did a good job passing my corner test. I stuck three Cheerios in tricky corners of my home, and it got two out of three, doing better than the latest Dyson vacuum. It managed to get the trickier two corners too; it skipped the third Cheerio to avoid bumping my bar stools. I also did a spill test with two spots of cherry juice in my home. It mopped away the first spill with no problem, but I did have to send it back out to finish cleaning the second spill. The UV Reveal did great with obstacle avoidance and has “NeverStuck Technology” to lift itself off obstacles, and it worked to get itself off the flat, long legs of one of my side tables. The vacuum finished a cleaning run in a good amount of time, cleaning my entire main floor in about 60 minutes, but it does go back out to scrub all the spots it sees on the floor. That took another 30 minutes for me, but I assume that would get shorter over time, the longer you live with this vacuum and have it cleaning up. Still, 93 minutes to run through four rooms and go back to do some scrub work is a solid time window.

Overall, this vacuum really shines on hard floors, but I also liked it on rugs and carpet if you have a mix of these in your home. It has an auto-empty base with a bagless debris system, so you won’t need to worry about purchasing debris bags to empty the docking station. The only downside is that the vacuum can learn only a single map, so it doesn’t work for multiple floors of your home unless you’re game for it to remap every time (which takes only a couple minutes, so it’s not a horrible experience, but the vacuum will also want the base station lugged up or down the stairs too). The suction is also a mystery; Shark has declined to comment on the exact suction. Still, we’ve loved low-suction vacuums before, and the results have been great.

This vacuum is one I refuse to part with, and while its retail price is technically $800, it's on sale enough in the $500 range that this has become the budget pick I'd easily recommend when it's on sale. The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is the newest update to Roborock's more affordable Qrevo line, which went without updates for years. The Qrevo 2 Pro is cheaper than the Curv 2 that launched in January 2026, and it still packs a ton of power, great navigation, and the same handy app. It comes with 20,000 Pa of suction, a FlexiArm mop that does a better job of corner cleaning, and a reversible side brush to help dislodge corner debris. I love seeing the arm reach out and get all the edges and corners around my house, especially underneath cabinets in the kitchen and bathroom.

The Qrevo 2 Pro also pulled ahead in some areas when compared against the similarly often-on-sale Eufy Omni C28. While the Eufy got itself stuck on cords in my bedroom, the Qrevo 2 Pro only attempted to eat cords without actually getting stuck on them. The Qrevo still isn't great at seeing small objects; it took my cat's toys for rides around the room, but they usually didn't get stuck or stop the vacuum. Both vacuums scored a 2 out of 3 on my Cheerio test, but the Qrevo 2 Pro got the harder fridge Cheerio with its FlexiArm mop. The Eufy did a little better on mopping, but neither vacuum did perfectly. I'm giving the Qrevo 2 Pro a 1.25 out of 2—one spill was just about gone, but the area around it was all slightly sticky, while the second spill was only half cleaned. It's hard to grade perfectly. It also occasionally leaves a little debris behind when it goes over thresholds that separate carpet from hard flooring, but it didn't have this issue when transitioning onto rugs.

This vacuum (and its base station) also looks good and is fairly quiet. (Except when it cleans on tile, which is a noisy experience as it travels across the grout divots. But it does a good job.) Both the base station and vacuum itself are quieter than the Eufy Omni C28, and it is especially pleasant if you let the Qrevo 2 Pro vacuum and mop separately. It takes longer than doing the combo cleans, but this vacuum pulled off doing both a separate vacuuming session and mopping of my massive first floor in two hours, which most vacuums still take for combo cleans.

We've loved the app and navigation from Roborock for years, and it still stands out among its rivals in this area. The Roborock only struggles to navigate on a C-shaped table with long, thin, flat legs it can't see against my wood floors. Besides that it does a fantastic job navigating around all kinds of furniture and never runs into anything the way I've seen more expensive vacuums do. It can map multiple floors of my house too. Ultimately, it's a great, well-rounded vacuum for the price.

If the Roborock Qrevo isn't on sale, this Eufy is the next best thing. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So previously recommended Eufy’s older X10 Pro Omni as a great robot vacuum without spending too much, and Eufy released the Eufy Omni C28 in February this year with a similar set of features and price point. The Omni C28 comes with nearly double the suction power of the older model, a self-cleaning roller mop instead of mop pads, and retractable detangling brushes.

It does a solid job mopping and vacuuming, but it has a shorter battery life, leaving it at only 37 percent after completing the four-room main floor of my house. This is a bit of a bummer, since this affordable vacuum can do multi-floor mapping. While it can store enough maps to clean all three levels of my home, it doesn’t have the battery life to do so. But it does charge fairly quickly, and I was able to still clean all three floors of my house in a single day—I just had to let it recharge a little at the base first. It went back up to 57 percent battery life after just 20 minutes in its docking station. It also tried to eat the cords near my bed, and luckily I was nearby to yank them free. If you get this vacuum, make sure your cords are clear of the vacuum's reach.

With my corner Cheerio test, this vacuum also got two out of three Cheerios, but it missed the trickier fridge-corner Cheerio. This is the hardest spot to get into, so I’m not surprised, but it does mean you’ll have to check those corners more with this vacuum. The cherry juice spill test also showed similar results: The first spot it reached was cleaned completely, while the second spot, which had more time to dry, still had some sticky residue left behind.

Overall, though, it’s a good vacuum for the price, especially since it packs multi-floor mapping, the capability to mop and vacuum, and good results all around for a vacuum that’s already usually on sale for around or under $500.

There are a lot of great robot vacuums out there. Here are a few others we’ve tried and liked.

Dreame L60 Ultra for $1,000: This vacuum did a good all-around job and packs a ton of good features, including dual flex arms, the EasyLeap System that lets it move over almost-2-inch tall obstacles, and 35,000 Pa of suction. This is a great one to buy if you have tall thresholds in your home thanks to that lifting feature, but otherwise, you could get a smarter vacuum for a cheaper price. This vacuum does promise dirt detection, but I never noticed it delivering on that promise. Still, my Dreame long-term tester commented that it's leagues quieter than her older Dreame vacuum, so it's a good upgrade choice if you like Dreame and want something quieter.

Dreame X50 Ultra for $800: If you have pets that tend to make one area of your home particularly hair- or debris-covered, this is the vacuum to get. The Dreame X50 Ultra has tons of great features, including double-roll brushes, side wands for edge cleaning, and a large-capacity docking station, but the real standout is the AI that can notice extremely dirty areas. It’s the most effective dirt- and obstacle-identification system that former WIRED editor Adrienne So has tried, and it will even remind her which areas it needs to clean more often (for her, that’s near her dog’s bed).

Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai for $800: The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai is a good robot vacuum overall, with a unique base station design that calls back to the Dyson stick vacuums and built-in AI to find spots and stains on your floor to scrub them away. It mostly worked, but I did prefer this feature in the Shark above, which has a similar starting retail price but is usually on sale. It’s also a little tall, so if you have builder-grade cabinets like I do, it might not be able to vacuum the toe kicks or underneath your Ikea furniture. (It got stuck underneath my Tolstad bed frame and was too tall to get underneath my Besta cabinet.)

Matic Robot Vacuum Bundle for $1,495: According to former WIRED editor Adrienne So, this vacuum is spectacular. It’s the only 10/10 rating she’s ever given a robot vacuum. Its six RGB infrared cameras do a great job making a 3D map, the single waste bag contains wet and dry debris, it does a great job cleaning toe kicks, and it was quiet enough to run without bothering So’s kids while they watched TV. That’s due to Matic’s lower suction power (only 3,200 Pa), but she didn’t notice any decrease in cleanliness as a result. It’s compact and square, giving it the ability to really get into corners. The only bummer is that it has expensive, proprietary waste bags. But those waste bags do have diaper salts, charcoal, and a HEPA filter, so you don’t have to replace the filters separately.

Narwal Flow for $849: WIRED’s Reviews team hasn’t always had success with Narwal’s vacuums, but when I tested this model late last year, I found it super easy to set up and get cleaning. I had no connectivity issues, installation was a breeze, and the app was easy to navigate. It did a good job cleaning my hard floors and rug, and even when I ran it right out of the box until it ran out of battery, it returned itself to its station to recharge and then resumed the task a few hours later, all on its own. The base station is also sleek and cute compared with the dark, bulky structures most have.

Roborock Saros 20 Flow for $1,300: If you're looking for something with serious suction, the Saros 20 Flow is my preferred choice out of Roborock's higher-power Saros line. I really like using it, and the roller mop does a good job mopping, but it only got one out of three Cheerios on my corner test and didn't manage to spot any stains on my floor, even with the promised built-in stain detection. It's the option I'd choose if you want a robot vacuum with great navigation and super-high suction (36,000 Pa) that won't deposit debris around the house like the Saros 20 tended to, but I think you'd be just as happy with a cheaper Roborock.

Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 for $1,000: This is another great option from Roborock and another part of the Qrevo line we've liked for years. The Qrevo Curv 2 came out in January and has similar strengths to the Qrevo 2 Pro above, but it has a roller mop called SpiraFlow instead of two individual mop pads. It also has similar struggles, with threshold debris and small objects being hard to spot. It's a good vacuum overall, and best on sale (which it often is!), but I'd pick my picks on sale over it.

A robot vacuum is an automated vacuum, usually shaped like a round disc, that moves around your house to vacuum (and mop, as many models these days include mopping) on your behalf. You might’ve heard some refer to these devices as “Roombas,” which is the brand that made the concept popular, but today just about every cleaning brand—from high-end Dyson to affordable Bissell—makes some kind of robot vacuum. They come with either a charging station or a larger docking station that can self-empty.

There are a few things most robot vacuums will need to work properly:

The Federal Communications Commission announced in late July that foreign-produced advanced robotic devices will now be included on the FCC’s Covered List. That list includes communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States—including robot vacuums (and similar devices like robotic pool cleaners and lawn mowers). While it won’t ban any models already on the market that have FCC approval, we’ll likely see a huge decline in available new models after this year. Models made in the US will be fine, but future vacuums from popular brands like Dreame, Eufy, Roborock, and more could be affected. For now, you'll still see vacuums launching from these brands, though, since FCC approval is given months ahead of product launches.

This decision comes from an interagency body in the White House executive branch called the National Security Determination, which has deemed automated robotic devices a security risk due to the data they collect, which could be used for surveillance and be remotely commandeered by “malign actors.” While the initial documentation describes humanoid robots and a recent case of a humanoid robot’s cybersecurity vulnerability to be remotely taken over, the official description of these robot devices will include robot vacuums and any devices meeting the following criteria:

Overall, robot vacuums themselves aren’t banned, but new models from companies based outside the US won’t get FCC approval and can’t be sold in the US. You don’t need to stop using any robot vacuum you have, but if you’re in the market for a new one, it’s better to shop sooner before availability starts to decline—and prices are likely to rise as supply falls.

Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV for $1,200: Dyson's newest version of the Spot+Scrub has a UV light to help its AI spot stains, and I was happy to see those stains reported in the app, but I couldn't tell if the vacuum actually did more detailed cleaning in those areas. That aside, I wanted to love this vacuum more than I did. My issue with the vacuum is how it did in regular cleaning sessions: It left pieces of popcorn behind when vacuuming on my downstairs rugs, didn't seem to ever get close enough to my walls for any kind of edge cleaning, and was too tall to get underneath cabinets or basic Ikea furniture around my house (but still smacked into that furniture over and over again due to camera placement). It also got a zero on my corner Cheerio test, failing to even get the Cheerio that just sits near a chair leg. I haven't tested either of the cheaper new Dyson robot vacuum options, but if this is how the best one does, I'm not inclined to.

Eufy S2 for $950: This robot vacuum has an intense-looking base station. However, I was disappointed it missed both the fridge and bookshelf Cheerios in my corner test, giving it only a one out of three. Both cherry stains were scrubbed away, but the floor near where the stains were felt sticky all over even with the stains ostensibly wiped away. It’s especially a bummer given the price point; it needed to do better to be worth such a high price tag.

iRobot Roomba Max 705 Combo for $800: The name Roomba is synonymous with robot vacuums for many people, but it’s actually a specific line made by iRobot. I really liked both the high-end look of the Max 705 Combo (not to be confused with the cheaper Max 705) and the overall job it did mopping and cleaning my floors. The app is great since it shows you a map of where the robot went, and it’ll also show you a little itinerary of which rooms it’s doing in what order. However, setup and any resetting you need to do is a long process, so be ready to commit and troubleshoot when you unbox it. My long-term tester has also reported that its mopping abilities have not improved over the six months it's been running in her house, but it does best with vacuuming and carpet.

iRobot Roomba Max 875 Combo With ThermaMist for $799: As Roomba’s new top-line robot vacuum and mop, this model features 35,000 Pa of suction, as well as hot steam to pretreat stuck-on stains. However, what really sold me was the “no pre-clean pickup” advertised on the box. I’ve got pet toys, my teen’s sports equipment and shoes all over the floor, cords, and loose rugs; other robot vacuums I’ve tried have struggled with my household. The Max 875, however, moved through my house with ease—in fact, I was quite impressed with how well it powered through even the toughest robovac challenges, like shoelaces and a maze of tucked-in chairs around a table. It did fine on pedestrian stains on my LVP floors, like spilled coffee, but even with the ThermaMist and repeated returns to the scene, the 875 Combo couldn’t fully clean an area with dried wet cat food. Setup was also pretty buggy—I followed the manual, but the vacuum took off before I could add it to the app and map my house, trying to clean a random area on 14 percent battery life. It would then return to the dock station, charge for five minutes, and repeat this process for well over an hour. When I did get it connected to the app, it said it needed an update but was unable to download it. I eventually got it to work by factory-resetting the machine and starting all over, but this process took more patience than I’d expect at this price point. —Kat Merck

iRobot Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $599: Like its fancier sibling, the Max 875 above, the Plus 678 had a bit of a buggy setup process that required several attempts and a factory reset. The Plus 678 also has the Max 875’s AI-powered stain pretreatment (though without the ThermaMist steam) and 30,000 Pa of suction for Roomba’s new “SealForce” technology, which lowers a skirt around carpets to suction deeper into the pile. I tested this with three different types of rugs—a regular-pile wool rug, a loose washable rug, and a low-pile faux fur rug. It did well on the first two, but failed on the third, becoming fully stuck. (Most vacuums can’t handle this rug, so I don’t exactly fault it for this.) Other than the setup mishaps—which included false “brush roller failure” messages and a mapping attempt that left it turning around in circles in the middle of an open room for 20 minutes—this is a serviceable mop-vac with a feature list that’s hard to fault at this price. —Kat Merck

iRobot Roomba Plus 575 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $499: After hearing about the futuristic Roomba growing up, I was excited to see one in action. During setup, I found that the battery cover unscrewed, but assumed it was intentional since no screws were included. It soon fell off, so I taped it; days later, it came off during cleaning and got lost, leaving the battery and cords exposed to debris and the wet mop. Not great. From the start, it struggled to map my home. Cleaning requires app routines, which I didn’t love, as sometimes I just wanted to be able to click a single room and go without having to create another routine. The routines were often ignored or stopped midway. A mop pad fell off on every single run, forcing me to retrace the machine’s path to find it in my home. It also got caught on cords and repeatedly tried to climb my cat tree’s base, getting stuck perpetually spinning until I had to manually move it. Edge cleaning was nonexistent; there was so much cat hair and dust near where the floor met the wall. After a month, it threw up and scattered debris whenever it crossed the ¾-inch thresholds to the bathroom, kitchen, and bedroom, so afterward I had to vacuum the mess it created—defeating the purpose. —Molly Higgins

Mova P10 Pro Ultra Gen2 for $360: This robot vacuum was solid, and especially did a good job with cleaning corners (it got a 2 out of 3 on the corner test, capturing both the stool and fridge Cheerios), but it did a poor job scrubbing away the cherry juice for my stain tests. One of the two stains was almost entirely left behind, and overall on casual runs of the vacuum it didn’t feel as if my floors were super clean. Still, if you’re looking for good corner cleaning, and carpets more than hard-floor deep cleaning, this is a solid robot vacuum for the price.

Roborock Saros 20 for $990: WIRED reviewer Adrienne So was mostly happy with this robot vacuum, as was I. She noticed the super-high suction (it hits 36,000 Pa) actually caused more debris to be left behind on her hard floors when it passed over thresholds; I didn't have this issue with the thresholds in my home, but instead I found debris on my hard floors immediately after having this vacuum clean them, with no threshold required. It also only got a one out of three in my Cheerio test, which isn't great for such an expensive vacuum.

Tapo RV50 Pro Omni for $400: After testing several robovacs that made me want to chuck them out the window, I had high hopes for Tapo’s new model that was released this summer. It promised over four hours of run time, dual-laser obstacle avoidance, DeepEdge mopping for corners and edges, and automatic floor detection to keep mops off carpets. But during more than two weeks of testing, it never mapped my home correctly or fully cleaned it. It couldn’t cross the ¾-inch raised thresholds into my kitchen or bathroom, and it mapped my bedroom but detected a phantom obstacle and cleaned only the 2-foot entryway. My kitchen, bathroom, and bedroom were never fully cleaned during testing. It’d be heading for the dock to wash mops or empty them and would forget to do the hall next or finish the living room and begin charging again. About half the time, the app asked me to map my home again, apparently forgetting the previous day’s map. During mapping, it sometimes started cleaning, got lost, and then announced it couldn’t find its dock, leaving me to locate and return it. When vacuuming, it sometimes left the mops at the station, returned for them, forgot, and began charging, thus ending its task. Not once did it successfully vacuum and mop my whole home. Online reviews are glowing, so perhaps I got a dud—but this experience was enough to make me want to clean by hand instead. —Molly Higgins

I test all robot vacuums in my three-story townhouse, where they clean across luxury vinyl plank (LVP); tile; carpet; and a large, low-pile rug. I have a dining table and four barstools to navigate, and both a cat and a child who create daily messes. I run the vacuum at least three times across the main floors of my home to assess its overall performance and note any recurring issues or errors it encounters. I do pick up my son’s toys, but I like to watch how the robot navigates the various chair legs and side tables throughout my home, and whether it sucks up the power cords beside my bed. I also like to see how much battery life is left after a run is complete on each level of my home.

My corner test, using three Cheerios in three corner (or cornerlike) spots.

I also set up an obstacle course of sorts. The first one is the corner test, created by three Cheerios placed in three tricky corners on the middle floor of my home: one in the corner of an Ikea Billy bookshelf toe kick, one underneath my countertops next to the fridge, and one next to a barstool chair leg. It’s how I test how well each robot vacuum gets into corners and underneath cabinetry.

My spill test, with two spots of cherry juice on the floor.

I also create intentional spills for these vacuums to clean up. I use maraschino cherry juice to create two spill spots, then use a paper towel to smear and thin the stain to better replicate a spill you might not have seen on your floors. Many robot vacuums have AI that promises to detect these kinds of stains, but so far, no vacuum has stopped and scrubbed both spots on its first try.

Can You Use Robot Vacuums on All Kinds of Floors?

You can, especially since there are so many mopping models now to better clean hard flooring. You can use these devices on anything from hardwood to LVP and tile, though I wouldn't recommend leaving smaller rugs out for these autonomous gadgets to get stuck on. Large, set rugs are fine, but bathroom and kitchen mats or any thin, easily moved rugs should be cleared out of the way and put in the wash instead of vacuumed by your robot vac.

How Often Do You Need to Maintain Your Robot Vacuum?

Taking good care of your robot vacuum will help it last. Here’s the debris-removal process you should follow for each robot vacuum style.

Make sure to review your robot vacuum’s manual for any other steps the manufacturer recommends you take regularly to keep the vacuum running for as long as possible. Many brands also have replacement parts, so you can swap out individual pieces like brushes without needing an entirely new vacuum.

Do I Still Need a Regular Vacuum if I Have a Robot Vacuum?

I recommend keeping some kind of vacuum on hand, though that can vary based on your home. If you have stairs, you’ll definitely still want a hand vacuum or stick vacuum that can easily maneuver and clean your staircase, while pet owners might want a vacuum that can clean upholstery. I prefer my Dyson stick vacuums for a good carpet clean, but your mileage may vary depending on your preferences. Either way, I think everyone needs a companion vacuum of some kind with a robot vacuum.

You don’t need it, but a self-emptying dock makes using a robot vacuum much easier. You aren’t fumbling with debris every time it runs, and having a single bag to remove or a bin to empty is much easier than pulling debris out of the vacuum itself. I’d even recommend choosing a stick vac with a self-emptying dock, as it just makes the whole experience so much easier.

How Does WIRED Obtain Robot Vacuums? What Happens When We’re Done Testing?

Almost all the robot vacuums we test are provided to us as press samples with the understanding that there is no guarantee of coverage or type of coverage. Most companies don’t want a used vacuum back, so we either donate them locally or have the top performers long-term tested to see how they last.

#356. Hims & Hers launches new peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

The new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October launched an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson said in a statement.

None of the company's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims said they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy."

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

The company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Hims said it plans to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The company also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The company said it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

"If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options."

However, Vinjamoori said there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

"We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he said. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a company of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead."

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He said Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight."

But health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," said Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body."

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, said Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?"

But he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The company says patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

In practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "big fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

There is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione showed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also said in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

#354. Emma Heming Willis shares family photos as daughter Mabel turns 11

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”

“How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

Heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

Willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage shows the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore

Heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”

In February, Willis’ family announced that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

“Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they said in an update shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

#353. Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains

Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws.

“It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), said Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer.

His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.

The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys said they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he says.

Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you plan it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month.

“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED.

More than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since it was launched in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products, like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne says.

The ICO stressed the importance of users understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended.

“If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” the CMA said in a statement.
