#352. German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

Two German film students confronted the American who won festival prizes with their animated movie. "The Talented Mr. F," their documentary on their fight against plagiarism, is now in the spotlight.

It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.

Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.

"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

When the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale quickly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.

US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.

Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

"We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it."

The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.

"We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person."

While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.

The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.

Later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.

"The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts."

"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story."

And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.

They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge."

The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.

Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

For the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.

And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.

Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.

The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.

They have a clear message for young creatives.

"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors."

What started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.

This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

#351. Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

#349. Thuma Dupes: Japanese Joinery Bed Frames That Stack Up (2026)

Silk & Snow (queen, with solid headboard)

Japanese joinery bed frames are bolt-free beds made from notched wood pieces that slide and click together to make a stable frame. Think Jenga, but with really nice, sleek wooden furniture. The advantages are many, starting with easy assembly that takes just a few minutes and requires no tools.

Thuma is the leading brand in this space, and we love its product lineup—several members of the WIRED Reviews team have tested Thuma beds, and all rave about them. However, they’re not cheap. A Thuma bed frame starts at $895 for a twin frame with no headboard, and the king-sized Thuma signature bed our testers loved costs $2,500.

Japanese joinery is a traditional carpentry method that uses only wooden components. Instead of nailing boards together, each piece of wood is carved so it snugly fits into openings carved into neighboring pieces—the “joints,” if you will. The tension and strong hold of the interconnected pieces create structural integrity.

It’s a pretty easy way to channel your inner Bob the Builder, and the finished bed frame looks stunning in its simplicity. However, we are always on the lookout for products at the intersection of high quality and low price—curious to see if any contenders could give Thuma a run for its money—so we researched and tested, and these are our findings.

Be sure also to check out our guides on the best mattresses we’ve tested, as well as the best pillows and bedsheets. You’ll need something to put on your new frame, after all!

Updated November 2026: We’ve added two new bed frames to this guide and ensured accuracy throughout.

DreamCloud (queen, with bamboo headboard)

I’m a longtime fan of DreamCloud mattresses, so it came as no surprise that the brand’s Japanese joinery bed frame is excellent. Like the mattress, this frame has numerous thoughtful details that stood out immediately.

DreamCloud made setup seamless. Each piece is labeled, and when it comes time to put it all together, take a gander at the endpoints of the long pieces. If you look closely at the joints where they intersect at the ends, you will see holes drilled into the top and bottom pieces. Small rods attach to the boards and fit into them, serving as a secondary mechanism to ensure stability. I find this impressive because the beams stack neatly into the grooves carved into the ends. In a word, it’s crisp. It’s a tiny detail, but the frame stayed virtually silent when I put a mattress on it or moved around in my sleep. I didn’t notice any shaking, either.

Another excellent feature is the frame’s center stability beam (crucial for preventing long-term sagging), which slides in last. This lets you avoid nesting it before closing the frame, unlike some other Japanese joinery models from different brands. It’s far more convenient.

Lining up the slats is the most challenging part of the process; you have to make sure everything is aligned perfectly. To help the process go smoothly, you’ll find wooden rods—similar to those on the ends of the boards—in the center of the bed, where you insert the slatted frames. They’re about the width of a pencil. Pop those slats in, unroll, Velcro to keep in place, and go.

You don’t need a headboard with this frame, but DreamCloud provided one for testing. Two square openings are located inside the top beam of the frame, right where your head would be. The headboard slides into these internal slots, which hold the end pieces and keep it upright. Foam block stickers are included to be attached last, so your wall doesn’t get scuffed up. All that, and still no tools necessary. Down to the details, people! And this detail you don’t want to skip—it’s around $449 for a queen. The headboard costs $299 extra, but even with that, it’s still far cheaper than luxury alternatives. You’ll also have two stain options: natural or a very pretty walnut.

That said, you’ll have to consider how many sleepers will use this frame and the weight of the mattress you’ll place on it. When I was testing new mattresses every week, two of the frame’s center support legs split right down the middle. Make sure you don’t screw them on too tightly, as I suspect the tension is what made the wood look like I had been chopping it with a small axe. Regardless, I was shocked to see this happen, and it is another notch on Thuma’s belt for heightened durability. —Julia Forbes

The Bamboo Bed Frame by DreamCloud ranges from $299 for a twin to $549 for a California king (frame only).

Silk & Snow (queen, with solid headboard)

Silk & Snow is another brand that I hold in high regard. Every time I’ve tested a mattress from the brand, it consistently packs quality for the price. This platform bed frame was no exception. There are two options: natural rubberwood and acacia wood. I opted for the latter, which is a medium-brown color. I thought that the stain was stunning, with a richness akin to a lovely latte. However, I really appreciate that they offer options not just in wood stain color, but also in the actual hardwood itself.

This frame arrived in four separate boxes. I liked this approach because it protected the wood stain’s integrity during shipping. Every other frame in this guide was packed into one box—not unlike a mattress-in-a-box, but heavier and longer. I actually preferred this route, as every box was also labeled for easy setup.

Like the DreamCloud frame, Silk & Snow’s doesn’t require tools or hardware to set up—it’s made entirely of wood. One thing I learned the hard way: Make sure the center beam is within the frame perimeter before fully closing it off. Then place the slats into the internal notches on the side rails, and it’s ready for a mattress. I had no issues with noise, shaking, or feeling unstable. It supported a mattress just fine, and I am still truly enamored with how the wood stain looked amidst my studio’s decor.

However, I do a lot of testing, so I’m constantly setting up and taking down mattresses, frames, and bedding. This is where having two people will be crucial, as I decided to do it all by myself for the sake of time, to the detriment of the frame. The frame got badly scratched up around the slatted portions where the corners of the boards stack together, due to my awkward solo assembly motions. I doubt you’ll be doing this as much as I do, but it was still a bit disappointing to see. Despite this, it’s worth recommending because I loved how it looked and performed. —Julia Forbes

The Silk & Snow Wooden Platform bed frame ranges from $550 for a twin to $900 for a king (frame only).

The Avocado City Bed Frame is a minimalist wood (blonde or walnut) platform frame with a completely tool-free Japanese-joinery assembly process. The same natural, nontoxic, and sustainable materials practices that guide the company’s mattresses are at play here as well.

The City Bed is regularly $1,299 for a queen, and it is the most affordable of Avocado’s bed options (though you have to factor in a shipping fee). It’s made from very nice, solid wood (I tested the walnut version). There’s an optional headboard that I did not test. The bed itself is attractive, fairly subtle, and unobtrusive. In fact, if your duvet is reasonably large, you may not even see much of the bedframe.

The frame fits together using interlocking joints with metal reinforcements. In my testing, it’s been solid and sturdy, with no squeaking or any signs of weak joints. It is a tight fit at times, especially at the four corners, and I had to tap it with a soft mallet to get it fully flush (which sort of defeats the no-tool promise, but you probably could have done the same with a copy of Infinite Jest or something equally solid). —Scott Gilbertson

The Avocado City bed frame ranges from $750 for a twin to $1,499 for a California king (frame only).

The Birch frame was the most basic of the Thuma dupes I tested. I was really excited about this one because the wood is sourced from the land of the pines, otherwise known as my home state of North Carolina. Poplar is a durable hardwood, and southern yellow pine is one of the harder pine woods. (I can attest to this because, for an eighth-grade science project, I tested the durability of regional woods.) The manufacturing partner is a certified member of the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC). The legs are made of a completely different wood, Appalachian maple. It also uses a soy-based resin to remain completely formaldehyde-free.

It arrived in two boxes, and setup was quick and easy—the step-by-step instructions were the most thorough of the bunch. With written descriptions and pictures, it’s hard to mess this up. Plus, you don’t need any tools to get this frame up and running. The outer boards were polished to maintain the gorgeous hue of the pine wood. However, be cautious when handling the inner slatted-board sections, as this wood is not finished. I got a small splinter and was not a happy camper. Next, I set up the bed and slept on it for a week—the standard amount of time I test mattresses. The first few days, this thing creaked and moaned like crazy. It didn’t feel stable, and I was shaken if I moved even slightly. By the end of the week, it seemed to fall into place and settle, so I no longer noticed the noise or motion.

I don’t want to discount this as a possible option, though, because the wood quality was what I wanted it to be, and so was the overall price. If you’re looking for a cheaper option for a guest room, upgrading your teen’s room, or furnishing a first apartment on a budget, this could work well for you. —Julia Forbes

The Birch Madison bed frame ranges from $749 for a twin to $978 for a California king.

Nectar Sleep (queen, with bamboo headboard)

I had never set up or slept on a Japanese joinery-style bed frame before testing this model from Nectar, and now I’m a true believer. The frame is made from bamboo, and assembly took just about 20 minutes with no tools required.

Putting it together was super simple: the four feet had cut-out notches where the frame slid into place, and you just needed to push down to make the pieces lock together—it’s essentially like putting together a giant set of Lincoln Logs. After sliding the footboard into the feet’s notches, you finish both sides the same way by pushing down into the notches. The middle section is springy and has a floating foot to adjust for the bed’s pressure, so no cumbersome box spring is needed. The slats are connected with Velcro and just need to be unspooled and adhered to the sides. I opted for a headboard that slides in from above and stays in place because of the cutouts on the head portion of the frame below.

I’m physically disabled, so putting together furniture with tools and nails or screws is nearly impossible. I recommend that anyone who’s in a similar position check out a Japanese-style bed frame, as it’s lightweight, requires no additional tools, and requires very little physical strength. Plus, this frame comes in two colors, has optional headboard attachments, a 60-night home trial, a two-year warranty, and free shipping. —Molly Higgins

The Nectar Bamboo bed frame ranges from $299 for a twin to $549 for a California king (frame only).

Here’s the thing: Thuma is still a Japanese joinery bed frame. Therefore, I’d be remiss not to include it on this list. While I can vouch that the options above are credible dupes, many of my teammates feel nothing beats the original in this case.

Thuma’s Classic Bed Frame is made from upcycled, sturdy rubberwood that comes in four finishes: walnut, natural, espresso, and gray. You can also choose different headboard variations, including all-wood, a pillow board (Italian wool and foam), or a hybrid of the two. The design’s not only beautiful, but it’s also backed by certifications such as UL GreenGuard Gold and CertiPur-US (if you opt for the pillow board).

WIRED Gear Editor Julian Chokkattu has had his Thuma frame for several years, and he notes it takes next to no time to set up. He also loves that it doesn’t creak or slide—just a strong sense of security while sleeping on it.

The Thuma Classic bed frame ranges from $895 for a twin to $1,495 for a California king (frame only).

Just like with the best mattresses we regularly test, each frame required a week of testing (not including naps) to evaluate night-over-night performance. This also allowed time for the frames to settle into place and perform alongside the bed each was paired with.

How Do I Set Up a Japanese Joinery Bed Frame?

Your bed frame should come with installation instructions, whether it features Japanese joinery construction or not. In the same vein, I recommend having someone assist you with the setup. As mentioned in our Silk & Snow review, this helps mitigate the risk of bumping and scratching your new furniture.

Are These Bed Frames Better Than Thuma’s?

We wouldn’t say better, just different. Each brand offers its own approach to creating a bed frame that adheres to the Japanese joinery method. This could include the type of wood used, the stains offered, the types of headboards you can pair it with, where it was manufactured, and, of course, the price.

#347. Investigators make progress in hunt for cause of FAA ground stop

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

While replicating the issue in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

The ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

Investigators said within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy said.

Since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

#345. Kohls is giving away free Kohls Cash and Sephora coupons on Black Friday — how to claim

TL;DR: Kohl's is giving the first 200 shoppers at each store a free $5 to $100 Kohl's Cash voucher on Nov. 27 (at 5 a.m.) and a $5 to $100 Sephora coupon on Nov. 28.

If you are looking to score free spending money for your holiday shopping run, Kohl's is giving early birds two big reasons to set an alarm this Black Friday weekend. For the first time ever, the retailer is pairing its classic Black Friday morning Kohl's Cash giveaway with a second wave of free Sephora at Kohl's coupons on Saturday, Nov. 28 — plus a four-day sweepstakes with $10,000 cash grand prizes.

Kohl's stores are closed on Thanksgiving Day (Nov. 26), though its main Black Friday Week sale is already live online. When physical stores reopen for the weekend, each giveaway comes with its own timing and same-day redemption rules, so here is how to claim yours.

Most Kohl's locations open bright and early at 5 a.m. local time on Black Friday, Nov. 27, though exact hours can vary by store. The first 200 customers through the doors at each participating Kohl's location will receive a free, instant Kohl's Cash voucher worth $5 to $100 — no purchase necessary.

However, you have to spend the promotional voucher in stores on that same day, and standard exclusions apply (it cannot be used on Sephora at Kohl's merchandise or gift cards).

If you would rather sleep past 5 a.m. on Friday — or you are mainly shopping for beauty gifts — Kohl's is running a second in-store giveaway on Saturday, Nov. 28. For the first time, the first 200 shoppers in line at participating Sephora at Kohl's locations will get an instant promotional coupon worth between $5 and $100 off at Sephora at Kohl's.

Just like Friday's doorbuster, the Sephora coupon is handed out on a first-come, first-served basis when doors open (limit one per household for shoppers 18 and older) and must be redeemed toward in-store beauty purchases that same day. Be sure to check your local Kohl's store page before heading out, since Saturday opening hours differ from Friday's 5 a.m. doorbuster schedule and not every Kohl's houses a Sephora shop.

Even if you skip the early-morning lines altogether, you can still enter Kohl's Black Friday sweepstakes from 5 a.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 27 through 11:59 p.m. ET on Monday, Nov. 30. You can submit a free entry either in stores or online — no purchase required — as long as you are 18 or older and live in the U.S. (limit one entry per person).

Before setting your alarm for Friday or Saturday, double-check your local store's exact opening time — and if you are mapping out a bigger morning route, check out our guide to Black Friday 2026 store hours to see when other major retailers open their doors.

#344. Best Gaming Mouse (2026): My Picks After Testing Dozens of Mice

Picking a gaming mouse can be difficult. There are countless metrics to factor in and a nearly unlimited number of mice with unique approaches in defining what's best. Quite honestly, it’s a market rife with opportunities for analysis paralysis to take hold.

That’s why I take the time to test countless gaming mice—to tell you what works and what doesn’t. I can’t say precisely which mouse will work for you—that’s dependent not only on technical specs but on your preferences, needs, budget, and hand size—but hopefully I can provide some insights into the top options out there, what's the best for specific types of gamers, and why I’ve picked them.

Be sure to read our other peripheral buying guides for more, including the Best Ergonomic Mouse, Best Gaming Headsets, Best Mechanical Keyboards, and Best Hall Effect Keyboards.

Updated November 2026: I've added the Razer Basilisk V4 Pro and Wallhack M-001. I've also included the Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike in my honorable mentions, reorganized the list, and updated prices.

The Razer Cobra HyperSpeed (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is far more reasonable and practical than most of the ultra-light options today. Instead of shaving down features and mass to make the simplest mouse possible, the Cobra Hyperspeed finds an ideal middle ground, maintaining features like RGB lighting, Bluetooth connectivity, and options for wireless charging. Despite that, it still weighs below 70 grams, a number that was unbelievable for even the most premium wireless mice a decade ago. Inside, it’s packing an optical sensor, optical switches, and an optical scroll wheel—all top-of-the-line parts that are some of the fastest and most reliable on the market. While the mouse is limited to 1,000-Hz polling with the included low-profile USB-A dongle (which I prefer for convenience), it can be upgraded to 8,000 Hz with the bulkier and less-convenient HyperPolling dongle, cutting out its only serious limitation.

Beyond that, this mouse can do practically everything. It works as a travel mouse, a permanent desktop solution, and is even compatible with Razer’s wireless charging pucks, which lets you charge the mouse using either the Mouse Dock Pro, which ups your polling rate to 8,000 Hz, or the HyperFlux V2 wireless charging mousepad. The simple, symmetrical shape is comfortable and easy to hold, with the curved buttons on top creating spots to rest your fingers, while the low, gradual curve feels natural for resting your palm. Plus, its near-symmetry means it can be used as an ambidextrous mouse in a pinch (although lefties will miss out on the side buttons).

While the price may be steep, Wallhack’s M-001 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is one of the best I’ve tested in a long time. Although the specs aren’t quite cutting-edge (the sensor is a bit outdated, and some of the internals are still mechanical instead of optical), every aspect of this mouse’s user experience has been fine-tuned to perfection. That's what sets it apart for me.

The mouse itself is made entirely from magnesium, and the outer shell doesn’t feature any of the large weight-saving cutouts used by similar mice from Corsair, AngryMiao, and even Razer. Instead, the upper is entirely solid, and all of the cutouts are on the underside of the mouse. Because of this, the battery can be swapped out within seconds.

Alongside the mouse itself, the M-001’s dongle is one of the best on the market. Instead of simply sitting on a desk, this dongle incorporates physical dials to adjust the mouse’s sensitivity and polling rate, and recharges the spare battery when not in use.

While it may be silly, my favorite feature of this mouse is the swappable batteries themselves. Similar to a Nintendo Switch cartridge or an SD card, the batteries feature a push-lock mechanism that’s robust, satisfying, and intuitive, improving significantly on the magnet or rotation-lock systems that other swappable mouse batteries use.

The Rival 3 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is a simple, no-frills gaming mouse. It’s lightweight, robust, and pretty much hits all the marks for gaming: Easy-access side buttons, clicky main buttons, underside RGB lighting, and a grippy rubberized scroll wheel. This SteelSeries mouse doesn’t innovate much, but like a Toyota Camry, it’s simple and reliable enough to get nearly anything done. At a price below $50, you’re getting all the performance you can realistically use for non-professional gaming. There aren’t any unnecessary features that add complication, and the mouse can be fully disassembled in under five minutes with a set of Phillips and Torx screwdrivers.

The Razer Viper V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is the latest installment in a long line of fantastic competitive mice, offering performance improvements across every metric. Along with top-of-the-line specs, optical sensors across the board, and a great symmetrical shape, the V4 also incorporates the same spherical dongle included with the Deathadder V4 Pro, which maintains its 8,000-Hz polling while adding LED indicators for information like connection quality, battery life, and DPI stage.

Using the exact same shape as the V3, this mouse is comfortable and intuitive to use. The shape is easy to move around, with small curves on the mouse buttons for your fingertips to rest, and the curvature of the sides creates natural spots for your thumb and pinky. The Razer Synapse software is one of the most powerful and intuitive on the market. There are customization options for mouse dpi, tracking distance, dynamic sensitivity, and even adjusting the mouse sensor to accommodate a rotated grip.

The only downside of the Viper V4 Pro is how uncompromising it is— there's no Bluetooth, and the included 2.4-GHz dongle requires a USB-A to USB-C cable (included) that runs to your computer, with no option for a smaller USB-A dongle (last seen on the V2). These decisions were made to lighten the mouse and improve connection quality, but they can be inconvenient if you need a wireless gaming mouse to pair with a laptop.

The Infinity .97 is one of the lightest mice I’ve tested at only 48.3 grams (without the removable rear panel, which adds 3.8 grams), and one of the sturdiest thanks to its magnesium upper shell. While the skeletal shape may look off-putting at first, it was far more comfortable and usable than I would have expected, especially when used with a fingertip grip. However, anyone dedicated to a palm or claw grip will likely be better served by a larger mouse with a sturdier back end.

Beyond weight, this mouse has fantastic specs: 8,000-Hz polling, optical switches, and a rating of 0.2 ms of latency all put it on par with Razer and Logitech’s best offerings. The most impressive feature by far is the removable and magnetically hot-swappable batteries that recharge using the mouse’s 2.4G dongle. This eliminates downtime from a dead battery and reduces the risks of long-term battery degradation and failure (assuming AngryMiao continues to sell spares).

While the styling is certainly more of an acquired taste, the large gaps result in a shape that’s rigid and better-looking than the usual uniform, hexagon-shaped holes. The shape is shockingly comfortable despite the gaps (which are placed to preserve typical touch points), and the removable rear “hatchback” panel finds a reasonable balance between a standard shape and the ultra-lightweight “fingertip mice” that have become more popular in recent years.

The software is also shockingly robust, with expected adjustments for DPI, polling, macros, and so on, alongside more granular adjustments like debounce speed, motion sync, ripple correction, and a Blast Mode that sets the mouse’s internal sensor to its maximum speed of 20,000 Hz. (It’s worth noting that the mouse still communicates with your computer at 8,000 Hz—this simply provides more data from the sensor to the mouse). Also, unlike some similarly-priced offerings, this mouse has both 2.4G and Bluetooth connectivity.

The Basilisk V3 Pro was a fantastic mouse, and the V4 Pro significantly improves the technical specs while maintaining some of the best features. Primarily, the V4 Pro has an absurdly-high 8,000-Hz polling rate and a scroll wheel with smooth, ratcheted, and “high-sensitivity” scrolling options. This mouse also maintains the same four-button layout on the side, and has a larger shape with an integrated thumb rest for comfortable long-term use.

As far as comfort and practicality, the Basilisk’s sculpted shape and thumb rest feel more like an office mouse than a gaming mouse, but the curved mouse buttons and smooth overall shape mean a claw grip still isn’t out of the question. The mouse wheel also has horizontal scrolling that’s activated by tilting it to the left or right, and the large number of programmable side buttons are great for both gaming and multimedia editing. While it’s still fairly hefty at 98 grams, this mouse is great if you’re either ambivalent about weight and want something more ergonomic, or if you prefer a heavier mouse. It might not be worth an upgrade when coming from the previous model, though, given the price.

The Pro X Superlight 2C is only marginally smaller than the standard Superlight 2, and weighs 51 grams, a 15 percent drop. It's essentially a scaled-down version. They are both capable of 8,000-Hz polling, use the same 44,000 dots-per-inch Hero 2 sensor, and have the same quoted 95-hour battery life. Because the 2C packs all this into a smaller package, it’s ideal for people with smaller hands, or anyone who primarily plays using a claw grip and doesn’t need the extra weight.

It's not a travel-size mouse, but I think the 2C is better suited than most ultralight mice on this list. It uses a small USB-A dongle that can slot into a removable panel on the underside of the mouse for transport, and the shell is fairly sturdy. I wouldn’t toss it into a checked bag at the airport or wedge it into a side pocket, but it should hold up for light travel.

A larger, sculpted alternative to the Viper V4 Pro, the DeathAdder V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a fantastic mouse that’s a tiny bit heavier, but potentially more comfortable than its smaller cousin. If you prefer the shape and feel of a sculpted mouse, this is a great alternative to Razer’s flagship competitive model that packs comparable performance and is equally-loaded with premium optical internals. The two share the same in-depth customization options, with adjustments for sensitivity curves, lift-off and landing distance, and the ability to adjust the mouse’s rotation for different grip styles.

The Deathadder V4 Pro also introduced Razer’s spherical USB-C dongle with three RGB lights that can be adjusted to display information like polling rate, battery level, connection quality, or DPI. While the colored light system can be a bit abstract, it provides functionality to an accessory that’s going to be on your desk no matter what, and makes it easier to keep track of the settings on this ultra-lightweight mouse. Plus, I find it looks a lot more natural than most dongles available today. Much like other competitive-focused options on this list, the only real issue with this mouse is the lack of Bluetooth connectivity, a weight-savings measure that makes sense for competitive use, but can be a bit annoying for certain users and setups that demand more flexibility.

Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike for $200: This is a major advancement in mouse tech, so much so that I’d consider it one of the most significant gaming mouse developments in recent years. This technology replaces the typical mechanical or optical switches under a mouse’s main buttons with analog switches, similar to those on a Hall effect keyboard, that allow for the actuation distance of the button to be customized. Because these linear switches no longer have a “click” sensation, the Superstrike pairs them with artificial haptic feedback. This activates when the button registers an input, and the intensity of the feedback can be customized across X levels.

However, I don’t personally like this mouse. The haptic feedback feels uncanny, since it shakes the entire mouse instead of creating a real “click” sensation, and the added complexity isn’t worth the relatively minor fine-tuning capabilities. However, I can recognize the benefits of the technology, and I can absolutely understand why some people might love this mouse.

Steelseries Rival Pro Wireless for $180: While the specs aren’t groundbreaking compared to other light mice, and the “ultra-polling” technology doesn’t offer a proven benefit over competitors, the Rival Wireless maintains the fantastic shape of previous installments in the Rival 300 line. If you’ve found other sculpted ultralight offerings from Razer and Logitech to be a bit lacking, this could be the option for you.

Razer Basilisk V3 Pro for $120: Razer’s previous installment in the Basilisk line is still a really solid option. This mouse is comfortable, convenient, loaded with features, and it looks sleek on any desk. It’s also featured in our Best Ergonomic Mouse guide, but it performs so well that I had to include it here. Razer’s optical sensor is capable of up to 35,000 dpi, and the mouse has polling up to 1,000 Hz (or up to 8,000 Hz with a HyperPolling dongle). As far as comfort and practicality, the Basilisk’s sculpted shape and thumb rest feel more like an office mouse than a gaming mouse, but the curved mouse buttons and smooth overall shape mean a claw grip still isn’t out of the question.

Corsair Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight for $200: When I first reviewed the new 36-gram Sabre, I was wowed by its weight but critical of its overly thin shell and flimsy construction. However, I accepted these as being a part of its innate nature as the lightest-possible mouse, and I’m incredibly glad that it exists. It’s a great option if you’re willing to sacrifice everything in the name of “simplifying and adding lightness,” as car designer Colin Chapman put it. But it's probably not the right choice if you want something that feels substantial or meaningful beyond that.

Corsair Sabre V2 Carbon Fiber and Magnesium for $170: While neither of these carry the same groundbreaking lightness of their predecessor (they both hover just below the 60-gram mark), they offer a much more refined design with premium materials and rigidity that’s unmatched by Corsair’s mainstream competitors. While they lag a bit behind in performance, they both feel fantastic to fling around a desk while providing a much more sturdy chassis that gives the impression they can withstand some serious use. Unless you really love the looks or science of carbon fiber, the less-expensive magnesium chassis is definitely the way to go in terms of both sturdiness and on-desk appeal.

Logitech Pro X Superlight 2 Dex for $150: This sculpted mouse predates the Deathadder V4 Pro by over a year and, because of this, the specs lag slightly behind it. However, the shape is just as comfortable, and the internals are still fantastic for anyone except the absolute most-discerning. The best part of this mouse is that, these days, it can easily be found on a significant discount. If you don’t want to shell out the extra cash for Razer’s latest model, or if you prefer Logitech’s software and styling, this is the mouse for you.

Corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE for $70: While MMO-focused mice aren’t finding themselves in the spotlight anymore (much like many of the MMOs that required numpads, and even numpads themselves, for that matter), there are still a few new models kicking around. The Scimitar is one of the most modern ones, adding adjustability to the classic numpad-on-the-side formula with a sliding rail to accommodate different grip styles and hand sizes. While this mouse obviously doesn’t compete with other models on this list in terms of technical specs or weight, it’s a really great mouse for the kinds of games that still necessitate having swathes of macros at your fingertips.

Steelseries Aerox 3 for $100: While it doesn’t have nearly the same weight or speed advantages as offerings from Razer and Logitech, the Aerox 3 is still a great mouse in its own special way. Weighing in at only 66 grams and being one of the only waterproof mice on this list (I literally ran it under a sink for a couple minutes to test this), this mouse is great for multi-user gaming computers, accident-prone individuals, and/or the poolside gaming setup of your dreams. Plus, built-in Bluetooth connectivity means you aren’t stuck with a dongle! However, 1000 Hz polling and 18,000 DPI do mean that, if you aren’t looking for something that’s more durable than average, you may be able to get a good bit more performance for a comparable price.

Logitech G203 for $20: Budget gaming mice often forgo a lot of the conveniences and performance you get out of nicer models, but the Logitech G203 never feels like it's lacking. The sensor has a lower maximum sensitivity than you'll get out of a more expensive offering—8,000 dots per inch—so if you need that top-end sensitivity, you'll want to look elsewhere, but it features six buttons, compatibility with Logitech’s G Hub software, and, most importantly, has RGB lighting. Those are all things you'd typically expect to pay more for.

Razer Viper V3 Pro for $100: The previous-gen Viper V3 Pro remains a good choice for competitive gamers, especially since it's selling for much less than the newer model. It remains an uncompromising mouse for lightweight, high-speed gaming performance. Despite being a couple of years old at this point, it still has competitive specs, the same great symmetrical shape, and some of the best-feeling buttons on the market. The battery lasts an incredibly long time (it’s rated for over 95 hours, and I didn’t need to charge it once during my testing). And with the included HyperPolling dongle, the mouse is capable of up to 8,000-Hz polling.

One of the cheapest things you can do to upgrade your PC gaming experience is to invest in a high-quality mousepad. If you’re a mouse-and-keyboard gamer, having the right surface for your trusty little rodent can be super helpful. Not only do you have a nice little area of your desk cordoned off for mouse use, but you also get a surface designed to be as friction-free and slick as possible—so you’ll be as quick as possible.

Harber London Professional Leather Desk Mat

Harber London Professional Leather Desk Mat for $239: Despite more than a year of use, this Harber London leather desk mat still looks exquisite. The pebbled leather is supple and has a nice texture, but your mouse will glide over it effortlessly. It comes in three sizes and three colors.

SteelSeries QcK Mouse Pad for $11: SteelSeries’ QcK mousepad is one of my all-time favorites. The medium size is perfect for most desks, even small ones. It’s well-made and doesn’t fray easily—cheaper mousepads often fray at the edges, which ruins the aesthetic a good mousepad can lend to a workstation.

Grovemade Wool Felt Desk Pad for $70: This doesn't seem like your usual gaming accessory, because it's not. It's a wool felt pad from Portland, Oregon, company Grovemade, and it's large enough to fit a keyboard and a mouse with room to spare. It feels soft and plush under your wrists, and all of the gaming mice on this list just glide over its surface; it's like they're sliding on glass. It's a big surprise, honestly. Not to mention, a felt desk pad adds an air of sophistication and style to any desk, without making it seem too uptight. The color looks amazing under RGB lighting in a dark room. It's an easy and affordable way to inject some unique style into your work (and play) space.

Here are a few features that really separate a gaming mouse from a regular came-with-my-PC kind of mouse:

Extra-sensitive optical sensors: Gaming mice should have more sensitive optical sensors that can detect smaller movements more quickly than a standard mouse.

More buttons: At a minimum, a good gaming mouse should have a clickable scroll wheel, a button for adjusting sensitivity, and two buttons where your thumb rests. Those extra thumb buttons can be lifesavers in competitive games.

Better buttons: They should also have higher-quality buttons, and more of them, than a standard office mouse. The left and right buttons should have individual switches inside, tensioned to register rapid clicks and reinforced to withstand more frequent clicks than a normal mouse. Top-of-the-line gaming mice often feature proprietary mechanical switches inside that give them a more tactile feel when you click.

Polling rate: For most games, the typical 1,000-Hz polling rate will be sufficient, but if you play a lot of fast-paced competitive games, where split-second actions can be crucial to victory, than you may get some benefit out of mice with faster polling rates.

Don't buy the DPI hype: Dots per inch (DPI) is a metric that describes a mouse’s overall sensitivity. A higher dpi means it can respond quicker, which is helpful in competitive online games. However, even if your mouse can go all the way up to, say, 20,000 dpi, most people (even in online games) keep their sensitivity around 1,000 to 1,600 dpi. More doesn’t necessarily mean better.

A major aspect when shopping for a gaming mouse is size. Using a mouse that’s too small for your hand can cause strain on your hand and wrist, while a mouse that’s too large can feel unwieldy and be difficult to move precisely. It’s important to measure your hand and take into account the grip style you plan to use.

There are three primary mouse grips: Palm grip, claw grip, and fingertip grip. Palm grip is typically considered the most accurate but least agile, and it’s how most people use their mouse day-to-day. Your entire hand sits on the mouse, with your palm resting on the back half and your fingers laid along the mouse buttons. Claw grip is more agile, but will sacrifice some accuracy and stability. For this grip, you rest the bottom of your hand against the mouse while bending your fingers into a claw-like shape, leaving a significant amount of open air between your fingertips and the back of your hand. Fingertip grip has the least contact and allows for the most agility, but also sacrifices even more stability. With this grip, your hand will hover over the mouse, with your fingertips resting on the mouse buttons, and your thumb and pinky finger gripping the mouse from either side.

For a standard mouse used with a palm grip, the best way to determine the correct size is to measure the distance from the tip of your middle finger to the bottom of your palm, and compare those numbers to an online guide. Rocket Jump Ninja has a helpful tool for this, which also provides measurements of the recommended mice for cross-referencing. Alternatively, I’ve found it helpful to hold your hand in an arc as if you’re holding a mouse, and measure the distance from the bottom of your palm to your fingertips to get a measurement you can directly compare to mouse length. This method can also work for claw grip, but since the bottom of your palm will be resting directly on the mouse instead of sitting at the back, I find it better to err on the side of caution and pick a mouse that’s a few millimeters longer than you need.

Mouse sizing is dependent on the type of mouse you’re looking for: Whether chasing lightness or portability, there are quite a few short and small mice on the market. Compact or fingertip-grip mice like the Razer Basilisk Mobile or the G-Wolves Fenrir won’t fit the standard recommendations of mouse measurements. Instead, for a mouse like this (or any mouse you plan to use with a fingertip grip), I find it best to compare the mouse’s width to the distance between your thumb and your pinky finger (or your ring finger, depending on how you hold a mouse) in a comfortable gripping position. A mouse that’s too narrow can cause strain on your hand, while one that’s too wide can be difficult to properly grip and move.

#343. Walmart hikes outlook as CEO tells CNBC retailer aims to keep prices low despite soaring fuel costs

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Walmart said global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

Walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can."

CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

"This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses."

Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said.

Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

Furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more."

The company on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey said Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start."

The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

#341. How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble

From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.

After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.

These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.

The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.

The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.

Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.

Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.

"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.

"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."

Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.

Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.

"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.

When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.

"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."

To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.

In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.

EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.

Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."

LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

#340. Gap names new Athleta CEO, says Old Navy turnaround is seeing signs of progress

Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

"I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode."

Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `

The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said.

The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth."

#338. A First Drive With the Fiat Topolino in New York City

The Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City. Fiat has been selling this tiny electric vehicle in Europe for three years, but it's now arriving in the US for $14,985 as a street-legal micromobility vehicle. Except it's more like a golf cart than a small EV.

It has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags. Classified as a “Low Speed Vehicle (LSV),” it can only operate on roads with a posted speed limit of 35 mph or less. (You still need a driver's license, and the Topolino must be registered and have auto insurance.) It also doesn't have a traditional EV charging plug; instead, it uses a 10-foot AC plug that works in any wall outlet—which can be tough if you're in a Brooklyn apartment.

“It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA. “This segment of micromobility—and that's really golf carts—based on the data we have, it's going to grow 28 percent in the next 5 years. People are driving golf carts not to play golf—they're driving them to go to the beach, to go to the clubhouse, to go get coffee, dinner, but they're all just generic. Topolino adds a little bit of that Italian flair and charm, and it's just so unique.”

That’s hard to refute. There's nothing like the Topolino on the market, EV or otherwise. Its adorable looks have drawn the attention of passersby, who've flicked me a thumbs up as I drove past, or pulled out their phones to sneak a quick pic. The Topolino (which is Italian for “little mouse,” and also what Italians call Mickey Mouse) comes with a lot of compromises, but I've had a blast piloting this thing around the city.

From my conversation with Waterhouse, it was clear that Fiat expects to sell more of these Topolino cars in places like suburban Florida. Gated communities, large residences with private land, homes by the beach—you get the idea. There are also hopes to turn the Topolino into a fleet vehicle for campuses and the like. But I wanted to see what it would be like in the bustling streets of New York City. After all, I already drive the Fiat 500 as my personal vehicle.

The Fiat Topolino, left, next to the already small Fiat 500, right.

The first thing that surprised me—other than the minuscule size, which you won't stop thinking about—is how plasticky the thing is. I leaned on it for a second and felt the plastic exterior sink in a little, which immediately made me realize the Topolino won't handle a crash very well; no crumple zones, no airbags—just seatbelts. So yes, don't take this thing on the highway.

It's built for two people and not much else. The passenger can stow a suitcase in front of them, and there's a rack on the back of the car to store another. But besides mesh pouches in the door frames and an elongated glove compartment on top of the dashboard that runs the width of the car, that's about it for storage.

I should also mention the Topolino comes in a few variants: The standard model I tried has full doors and a fixed glass roof, but there's an Open Air model with a roll-back soft-top roof, and the Dolce Vita model has rope doors (aka no doors) and the soft-top roof. You can buy the car in mint, orange, or brownish-gray.

Thankfully, despite my 6'4" frame, I fit quite comfortably in the Topolino. I do have to swing my leg under the steering wheel as I get in, and the seats are a little firm, but the inside feels quite roomy. Only the driver's seat can move forward or back—the passenger seat stays put, and you cannot adjust the steering wheel height.

The asymmetrical, reverse-hinged doors are very unique. The driver's side opens outward from the front, and the passenger door opens the opposite way. There's also a button on each side to open the door, and weirdly, to get out, you pull a fabric strap. Now, the driver-side strap is to the left of the steering wheel, which makes sense, but the passenger-side strap is in an awkward spot behind the seat, near the seatbelt strap. A few of my passengers found that annoying. Also annoying is that you need to use the key to unlock both doors individually—no auto-unlock button plus no key fob. (The car starts with a second key.)

The horizontally split, manually hinged windows flip up, but on rougher roads, they tend to flip back down. You can adjust the small, circular side mirrors and the rear-view mirror, which also doubles as a backup camera display. I have found the backup camera mostly useless, especially at night, when it's just really hard to see what’s going on.

Good thing visibility in the Topolino is excellent, so it's really easy to swing your head around. Unsurprisingly, you can park this thing anywhere. I've parallel parked the Topolino in several tight spots that no other car can fit in, and the lack of parking sensors or the lackluster backup camera didn't bother me. In a city as crowded as New York, that's incredibly valuable.

You should know there's no air-conditioning or heating. There's a windshield fan to defog the windows, which, along with the single wiper and wiper fluid, was useful on cold, rainy days. But in the winter months, you'll have to bundle up, or in the summer, affix a battery-powered (or USB-C) fan to the dashboard. On the dash, you have a simple instrument cluster that shows speed and remaining range, and a built-in phone mount to the right.

You can store luggage on the rack—there's no trunk.

Turn the key to start the car, disengage the parking brake, and tap D or R to start driving. There's no power steering, so turning the wheel requires a little more force than you're used to, and the turn signals don't automatically disengage after you turn. Still, the car feels very responsive. The 8-horsepower electric motor feels fairly quick when you put the pedal to the metal, though you quickly hit the Topolino’s top speed. Good thing the default speed limit in New York City is 25 mph.

But as you start driving, you'll experience arguably the worst thing about the Fiat Topolino: the sound. Because of federal regulations around electric LSVs, the Topolino has a pedestrian alert sound—the kind of angelic hum you might have heard when an electric car is reversing or rolling up to a stop sign. Except the sound is constant, and it gets louder the faster you go. I'm not sure why it's so loud in the car. It feels like it's alerting me more than pedestrians around me.

The sound only disappears if you go past 22 mph, which isn't often, since streets in most cities have a stop sign or traffic light after every block. The first time my wife and I rode in the car, we could barely hear each other talk over the hum. You get used to it over time, but it's very annoying. You can try playing music over it, but the car has no speaker system. Instead, Fiat sells a pair of Monster Bluetooth speakers that you can magnetically stick to the top frame of the car. That works OK, but I didn't like having to keep them charged, so when they died, I played music from my phone. It was sad.

The ride is a little stiff. I drove over one of the worst roads in Brooklyn (Broadway), and you could feel every single bump. When I drove with my brother, they often just exclaimed “Jesus!” every few minutes. Cobblestone was equally pretty bad. But it's doable, and on well-maintained roads, the Topolino was a smooth ride.

New Yorkers rejoice! You legally cannot drive this car into New Jersey. (As if you needed a reason.) All of the bridges and tunnels to the Garden State have speed limits higher than 35 mph. However, I could take the East River bridges to go from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and I did exactly that. Driving over the Manhattan Bridge was a little terrifying when I was holding up a few cars in my lane and everyone decided to race around me. But I got a few thumbs-ups along the way, which helped. Everyone finds this car cute, which goes a long way toward how people treat you on the road.

As for range, it's not great. I wish it were closer to 80 miles instead of 46 miles, especially at this price. It's perfect for quick hour-long round trips around the city; anything longer will give you range anxiety. That trip over the bridge? I went from Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, to Lower Manhattan and back (around 12 miles). The indicated remaining range went from 46 miles to 30 by the time I got home.

Recharging takes around five hours from zero to full, and the charging cord is built into the car near the passenger-side door. Annoyingly, the 10-foot cable isn't retractable, so you awkwardly have to stuff it back into the door frame when you're done. But the bigger issue is the length. And the standard AC plug. EV charging stations don't typically have AC outlets like the ones in your home. And 10 feet is far too short to reach any apartment or residence in New York City.

Charging the Fiat Topolino requires a standard wall outlet—and, in Brooklyn, probably a long extension cord.

I bought a 50-foot extension cord and ran the cable from my outdoor parking spot to my backyard outlet. It worked perfectly well, but I'm also an outlier, with access to a parking spot and a backyard. Most people don't have those luxuries, so you'll need your own solution.

Initially, after my first ride with the Topolino, I was apprehensive. It felt like I was sitting in a plastic box on wheels, with a blaring sound that wouldn't stop, and every big bump sending a shock into my body. After a week, I was driving the thing everywhere, hand dangling out the half-window, fist-bumping other drivers in bumper-to-bumper traffic, and parking in the tiniest available spots around Brooklyn. Now, a week without the little mouse, I miss it dearly.

It's far from the perfect city car. There are small things I would change to improve the overall rideability. And like the Fiat 500e, it's way too expensive. But as someone who likes their car to stand out, I find so much of what's available in the US market uninspiring. The Topolino breaks the mold. We need more small cars like it.
